title: The Next Frontier: Harnessing Technology to Close the Justice Gap (LSC Technology Summit Report 2024-2025)
author: Legal Services Corporation

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The LSC report accepts selective, human-governed deployment rather than indiscriminate automation and materially extends the cluster with an access-to-justice implementation blueprint: practical use cases, safe experimentation, shared guidance, scalable tools, organisational capacity and impact evaluation. It also recognises reliability, confidentiality, resource and measurement constraints, while stopping short of demonstrating population-level remedy outcomes.
qs: LSC should lead and coordinate **responsible AI innovation and broader technology adoption** in legal services by promoting experimentation, collaboration, and the development of shared tools, policies and practices across the access-to-justice community.

This means emphasizing practical and scalable tools and solutions that can save time, increase efficiencies and deliver other short-term improvements in the capacity of legal services organizations to meet client needs.

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The LSC report supports the cluster’s calibrated proposition: AI may expand legal-aid capacity and self-help access, but adoption should focus on bounded, lower-risk uses and be accompanied by safeguards for accuracy, security and confidentiality. Its claimed benefits are largely prospective or pilot-specific rather than evidence of improved population-level legal outcomes, and it gives limited attention to direct users’ verification burdens or access without effective remedies.
qs: Said Nori: “Every minute saved because of AI tools is a minute we can use to help more people.”  At the same time, participants in the summit discussions were clear-eyed about the challenges and risks of making AI technologies and tools more integral to the delivery of legal services for low-income populations.

By promoting responsible experimentation, fostering collaboration across sectors and investing in shared tools and guidance, LSC can help legal services organizations navigate the risks while seizing the benefits of AI innovation.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The report supports the cluster’s core proposition that responsible legal AI adoption should focus on bounded, lower-risk tasks, active risk management, training and institutional support rather than autonomous replacement. Its legal-aid evidence reinforces selective workflow deployment and organisational complements, though it does not directly examine apprenticeship or long-term competence risks.
qs: At the same time, they expressed support for an active role for LSC in collaborative efforts to explore and resolve issues around the safety, accuracy and security of these systems.

st.t: Legal-aid technology: Infrastructure matters beyond tool grants
st.an: The source directly endorses the cluster’s proposition: technology and AI are supporting infrastructure rather than standalone justice-gap solutions. Its seven-part agenda emphasizes organizational capacity, shared learning, responsible experimentation, scalable self-help, flexible funding, and outcome-focused evaluation, while treating aggregate access gains as an ambition rather than an established result.
qs: Technology alone will not close the justice gap in the U.S.

While the summit yielded robust debate on many issues, there was wide agreement that LSC can make an enormous difference by helping grantees build their technology capacity, experiment safely, scale successful solutions and adopt practices that make the delivery of legal services faster, more efficient, and more equitable.

kp.k: Technology supports, but cannot alone close, the justice gap
kp.d: LSC reports that its latest Justice Gap Report found low-income Americans received no or insufficient legal help for 92 percent of their civil legal problems in 2022. Recommendation 7 separately reports that grantees turned away 49 percent of requests received in the prior year. The report advocates both connecting more people to professional assistance and improving self-help, explicitly treating technology as a supporting intervention rather than a complete solution.
qs: LSC’s latest Justice Gap Report showed that low-income Americans did not receive any or enough legal help for 92 percent of their civil legal problems in 2022.
Technology alone will not close the justice gap in the U.S. today, but it can and must play a vital supporting role.
LSC’s 2022 Justice Gap report found that LSC grantees had to turn away one of every two (49 percent) of the requests for legal help they received in the prior year.

kp.k: Recommendations reflect stakeholder deliberation, not demonstrated systemwide AI impact
kp.d: The seven recommendations emerged from a two-year summit process involving a February 2024 workshop of more than 50 technology and legal services thought leaders, four workgroups, interviews and focus groups. They constitute a proposed roadmap for LSC’s 130 independent nonprofit grantees and the wider access-to-justice community, accompanied by individual project examples.
qs: In this report, LSC presents seven recommendations that emerged from this two-year summit process.

The 2024-2025 LSC Technology Summit process kicked off with a full-day workshop of more than 50 technology and legal services thought leaders ahead of LSC’s Innovations in Technology conference in Charlotte, North Carolina, in February 2024.
The summit process also involved extensive stakeholder interviews and focus groups with field experts and grantees, plus strategic conversations among LSC leadership and staff

kp.k: Technology investment requires leadership and organizational change
kp.d: LSC argues that constrained budgets and organizational capacity cause legal services providers to treat advanced technology as an unaffordable luxury. It recommends leadership training, technical assistance, assessment of technology capacity and funding incentives to integrate technology into core service delivery. As broader nonprofit context, it cites a 2024 NTEN and Heller Consulting survey in which 45 percent of more than 300 nonprofits reported spending too little on technology; this is not a legal-aid-specific finding.
qs: In a 2024 survey by NTEN and Heller Consulting, 45 percent of more than 300 diverse nonprofits surveyed said they were spending “too little” on technology.
We need to help people see that you need leadership and systems and structures in place so this becomes how you do business
The key to success is not to make technology prioritization an added burden for grantees, but to act in a supporting and facilitating role

kp.k: Document automation produces reported time savings and reduced tedium
kp.d: The report describes Southern Minnesota Regional Legal Services integrating LegalServer with Gavel to reuse existing client data in family-law and public-benefits documents. Some preparation times reportedly fell by half or more, including a form reduced from 13 minutes to five. Staff reported less repetitive work and more time with clients. This example concerns document automation, not a demonstrated generative-AI effect.
qs: Instead of retyping client information into each new form, the team built a bridge between their case management system, LegalServer, and a document automation tool called Gavel.
In some cases, SMRLS was able to reduce document preparation time by half or more.
For instance, a family law form that used to take 13 minutes now takes just five.
staff report that automation reduces the stress and tedium of manually reentering information

kp.k: Shared infrastructure should reduce duplication and support replication
kp.d: Summit participants report difficulty identifying useful technologies and learning how peers implemented them. LSC recommends a centralized resource hub, better documentation of TIG projects, peer learning and reusable tools, including lessons from unsuccessful projects. Its Technology Baselines cover 15 categories but do not provide tailored implementation instructions. Open-source DLAW website improvements and publicly shared document-assembly code illustrate existing approaches to reuse.
qs: All too often, however, promising solutions are not shared in ways that could support other organizations to adopt — and adapt — those same technologies for the benefit of their clients.

What the baselines do not offer is tailored, step-by-step guidance for LSC grantees and other legal services organizations on how to make the most of the recommended technologies in the context of their day-to-day work.
The open-source upgrades and collaborative development model ensure that legal aid organizations in other states can adopt these enhancements without duplicating effort or cost.

kp.k: Funding should match rapid technological change and permit experimentation
kp.d: LSC reports 923 TIG grants totaling more than $92 million since 2000 and roughly $5 million in annual grants. Participants identify duplication among individually funded projects and application-to-start delays of up to 10 months to a year. Proposed reforms include rolling deadlines, fast-track planning and proof-of-concept grants, collaborative sandbox cohorts, greater weight for scalable solutions and exploration of funding non-LSC entities. These are options under consideration, not enacted funding changes.
qs: The TIG program has awarded 923 grants totaling more than $92 million since its inception in 2000.
The TIG program offers roughly $5 million in grants each year in three categories:
From start to finish, the process of applying for a TIG, getting a grant approved and beginning work on the grant can take as long as 10 months to a year.
There is a fear out there that if we fail we might not get another TIG, but failure is crucial to learning

kp.k: Data capacity is essential to service improvement and accountability
kp.d: LSC recommends investment in dashboards, automated collection, performance analytics, training and project-level data strategies. Participants identify limited resources, cultural resistance, inconsistent data standards, confidentiality concerns and inaccessible court data as barriers. The report describes Cleveland legal aid’s website-referral analysis contributing, alongside other information, to research that played a role in a policy eliminating debt-related driver’s license suspensions.
qs: many legal services organizations do not systematically collect data on client outcomes, service efficiency or impact.
different entities often collect and categorize data differently, making it hard to aggregate or compare data across systems.
Too often, there is no data strategy at the outset, which significantly impairs the ability to do an adequate evaluation later (or along the way, which is preferred).
The report and its findings, in turn, played a key role in the development of a new state policy to eliminate debt-related driver’s license suspensions.

kp.k: Evaluation should measure learning, operations and longer-term client outcomes
kp.d: Participants argue that insufficient evaluation funding, short grant periods and unclear or inconsistent measures constrain assessment of technology projects. LSC recommends evaluation formats matched to project scope: rapid assessments, rolling reports, developmental evaluations and selected longitudinal or post-grant studies. It also proposes adequate evaluation budgets, shared methods, coordination with other funders and using lessons from both successful and unsuccessful projects in future grantmaking. Operational improvements may be worthwhile even without a direct client-service effect.
qs: the grant period for most TIG grants is often too short to allow for meaningful measurement of their long-term impact on grantee operations, client experiences and self-represented litigants
So if a technology project doesn’t necessarily touch the client service side, it doesn’t mean it’s not a worthwhile project that can and should be measured in some way.
Offering more flexible evaluation formats and timelines would allow grantees to better measure what matters — when it matters — while creating more relevant and timely insights for LSC and the field.

kp.k: AI is proposed for both legal and administrative tasks
kp.d: Summit participants identify intake, routing, client support, motion and brief drafting, scheduling, transcription and automated communications as promising uses. Sateesh Nori frames efficiency gains as additional capacity to assist people. The report presents this as a potential mechanism for expanding legal aid rather than evidence of workforce reductions or a quantified increase in service capacity.
qs: client intake, routing and support services (i.e., “getting people to the right places more efficiently”); and more advanced legal tasks like drafting motions and legal briefs.
Participants also noted enormous potential for AI in improving time management and operational efficiency for attorneys, such as scheduling, transcription and automated communications.
Every minute saved because of AI tools is a minute we can use to help more people.

kp.k: AI accuracy and confidentiality risks constrain adoption
kp.d: Participants express skepticism about factual reliability and concerns about ethics, security and confidentiality, including AI meeting transcription. Nate Vogel reports that people do not yet consider the tools sufficiently reliable for generating factual information. LSC recommends model privacy and governance policies, safe-use guidance, training and secure experimentation environments, alongside collaboration to address accuracy and security.
qs: People feel that if the goal is to use these tools to generate factual information, then they aren’t good enough yet.
An example is the growing use of AI-powered meeting transcription services and their implications for client confidentiality.
LSC should create model data privacy and governance policies to help address questions and issues that may be barriers for legal services organizations to experiment with new technology solutions.

kp.k: Early AI evidence emphasizes bounded, lower-risk applications
kp.d: The report cites a 2024 Berkeley Law study involving 91 legal services attorneys given one to two months of access to paid generative-AI tools. The quoted study reports that participants managed risks by concentrating on summarization, preliminary or confirmatory research, first drafts and accessible-language translation. Separately, LSC reports 570 AI Peer Learning Labs enrollees as of summer 2025 and survey responses from more than 450 registrants; the supplied text does not give the numerical results shown under the survey-chart headings.
qs: For a 2024 study of AI use in legal services, Berkeley Law assembled a cohort of 91 legal services attorneys who received one to two months of access to paid generative AI tools.

While concerns remained, pilot participants were able to manage risks by focusing on lower-risk applications like document summarization, confirmatory or preliminary research, the production of first drafts, and translation from legalese or English into more accessible formats.

As of summer 2025, LSC’s AI Peer Learning Labs initiative had enrolled 570 legal aid providers in a community dedicated to sharing materials, case studies and lessons about incorporating AI-enabled tools into their work.

kp.k: AI adoption should prioritize practical experiments and shared governance
kp.d: LSC recommends repositories of AI case studies and implementation guidance, continued peer learning, technology sprints, a possible ethics advisory panel and secure sandboxes. Participants emphasize concrete everyday use cases and short experiments rather than hype. Quinten Steenhuis suggests quick-start, quick-stop micro-experiments because effective legal-services uses remain uncertain; Margaret Hagan calls for criteria to assess pilot results.
qs: The focus has to be on effectiveness
If we can create solutions that solve day-to-day challenges for attorneys and remove barriers to client service, that is a good strategy.

Micro-experiments, with quick start and stop phases, might be a more beneficial approach than longer-term projects, given that no one quite knows the best way to use this tech, especially in legal services.
As people launch new pilots, we need to make sure they are asking the right questions

kp.k: AI projects combine staff assistance and public-facing navigation
kp.d: The report describes planned or developing systems rather than uniformly completed deployments. Lone Star Legal Aid’s 2024 chatbot project covers staff legal research, internal HR/IT support and decision-tree client navigation. North Carolina’s Justice Hub is intended to integrate conversational AI, forms, videos and financial screening into intake. Louisiana’s project links legal-needs screening and referrals to the 211 network. Separately, Lone Star’s existing LACI application monitors legal changes and alerts staff to update self-help content.
qs: The second project is a suite of AI-powered chatbots that serve three key functions: a legal research assistant for staff, an internal HR/IT help tool and a decision-tree-based client chatbot to guide users to legal services, self-help resources and social services.
The Hub will incorporate conversational AI, automated forms, self-help videos and e- screening financial tools to streamline the intake process and provide immediate legal information.

LSLA also created the Legal Aid Content Intelligence (LACI) web application, which automatically monitors laws and regulations for changes and alerts staff when updates are needed to self-help legal information.

kp.k: Self-help tools address unmet need beyond attorney representation
kp.d: LSC identifies a distinct shortage of usable self-help resources for people who cannot obtain assistance or do not seek it. It recommends expanding mobile-friendly, plain-language tools, AI chatbots, intelligent document assembly and triage for self-represented litigants, especially in housing, family law and consumer debt. These tools aim to support navigating procedures and completing forms, not merely finding information.
qs: There’s also a self-help gap where people lack high- quality, usable tools to navigate the legal process themselves
The goal is not solely to provide expanded access to legal information but also to help people navigate complex systems, complete forms and prepare for court on their own.
This includes funding and promoting more experiments and projects that use AI- driven tools to provide real-time guidance to self-represented litigants

kp.k: Reported self-help uptake does not establish broader legal outcomes
kp.d: The report records over 11,500 unique visitors and more than 3,000 conversations over three months for Community Legal Services of Mid-Florida’s guided-navigation chatbot, with high satisfaction reported by staff and users. Lone Star’s guided interviews reportedly helped over 100,000 individuals start legal processes. These are engagement and service-use findings; the report recommends future self-help investments showing measurable access improvements and client outcomes.
qs: Evaluation of the project showed strong engagement with the chatbot, with over 11,500 unique visitors and more than 3,000 conversations in just three months, primarily focused on family law, housing and consumer issues.
Staff and user feedback indicated high satisfaction with the chatbot’s ability to direct users to relevant self-help materials and legal information.
To date, they’ve helped over 100,000 individuals start legal processes with confidence and clarity.
LSC, through its TIG funding, could support the development of innovative self-help tools that show measurable improvements in access to legal services and improved client outcomes.

kp.k: Accessible design and community intermediaries extend technology’s reach
kp.d: LSC recommends involving self-represented litigants in design and testing, multilingual materials, screen-reader compatibility, simple navigation and audiovisual guidance. It also advocates interoperability with courts, libraries, statewide portals and social-service networks. Public kiosks address connectivity, transportation and geographic barriers; Arizona had installed six of eight planned kiosks by mid-2025. The report proposes exploring how self-help technology can support community justice workers and other non-lawyers delivering information and limited-scope services.
qs: LSC can support and encourage grantees to engage clients and self-represented litigants in the design and testing of those tools.
As of mid-2025, CLS had completed development of the kiosk interface and installed six of eight planned kiosks.

Community justice workers are trained and trusted community intermediaries that can provide legal information and limited- scope legal services to low-income clients, especially in rural and remote areas.

LSC should explore and share how technology-enabled self-help legal tools can support the provision of legal information and limited-scope legal services by community justice workers and other non-lawyers.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: LSC and summit participants present AI as a means of expanding civil legal aid capacity and self-help access, not as a sufficient solution to the justice gap.
pts.d: LSC states that legal services programs are already experimenting with and using AI to increase efficiency and expand access to legal information and assistance. It predicts further benefits from responsible experimentation, shared tools and scalable deployment. The report's overarching qualification concerns technology generally: technology supports both access to expert advice and representation and better self-help, but cannot close the justice gap alone. It does not predict lawyer job losses, changes to commercial law-firm staffing or a quantified reduction in unmet legal need.

pts.k: Sateesh Nori and other summit participants anticipate AI improving intake, routing, drafting and administrative work, with saved time redirected toward helping more people.
pts.d: Nori describes potential changes to case management and service delivery. The report attributes to Nori and other participants prospective uses in intake, client support, motions and briefs, scheduling, transcription and automated communications. This is primarily an augmentation claim about making legal aid staff more effective, rather than a forecast of replacing them. Scheree Gilchrist argues that adoption should focus on practical tools that remove day-to-day barriers to client service.

pts.k: LSC describes concrete AI-enabled projects intended to improve screening, referrals, intake and round-the-clock support.
pts.d: Southeast Louisiana Legal Services is developing a screening and referral application connected to Louisiana 211, with AI-driven legal issue search and a smart referral algorithm. Legal Aid of North Carolina's Justice Hub is intended to combine conversational AI with forms, videos and financial screening to streamline intake and provide immediate information. Lone Star Legal Aid's 2024-funded chatbot suite covers staff legal research, internal HR/IT assistance and decision-tree-based client navigation. The report describes these functions and intended benefits; it does not report measured AI-specific results for these projects.

pts.k: Summit participants propose generative AI as a way to extend useful self-help to people legal aid cannot represent.
pts.d: Maya Markovich argues that AI could answer clients' questions and direct them toward self-help next steps, especially when organizations must turn them away. LSC recommends experiments with real-time guidance, legal chatbots, intelligent document assembly and triage to explain issues in plain language and help users navigate the legal system. These are proposed client-facing assistance functions, distinct from the report's staff-augmentation uses. The report does not establish that unsupervised AI legal advice is safe or effective.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The central AI claims rest chiefly on stakeholder expertise, implementation examples and a short Berkeley Law pilot, rather than quantified evidence of justice-gap reduction.
pts.d: The 2024–2025 summit included a workshop of more than 50 leaders, workgroups, interviews and focus groups. Its recommendations synthesize those participants' experience and judgments. The report also cites a 2024 Berkeley Law study involving 91 legal services attorneys given one to two months of access to paid generative AI tools. The quoted study reports risk management through lower-risk uses, including summarization, preliminary or confirmatory research, first drafts and translation. The supplied text gives no controlled outcome estimates, model benchmarks or AI-specific productivity measurements from that study.

pts.k: Adoption indicators and unmet-need statistics establish context, while reported successes of broader technology should not be treated as AI-specific findings.
pts.d: By summer 2025, LSC's AI Peer Learning Labs had enrolled 570 legal aid providers; its participant survey drew responses from more than 450 registrants. The supplied text contains chart headings but not chart values, so it supports no precise adoption-rate estimate. The report cites the 2022 Justice Gap Report's finding that 92 percent of low-income Americans' civil legal problems received no or insufficient help. Separately, a Florida guided-navigation chatbot recorded more than 11,500 unique visitors and 3,000 conversations in three months, with favorable staff and user feedback, but the spotlight does not identify it as generative AI. Likewise, document-automation time savings elsewhere in the report are not explicitly attributed to AI. These examples support the broader technology narrative, not a measured causal claim about generative AI.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The report distinguishes current pilots and early adoption from prospective scaling, without setting a date or numerical target for AI's ultimate impact.
pts.d: The report is situated in the 2024–2025 summit process: Lone Star Legal Aid received AI project funding in 2024, LSC launched AI Peer Learning Labs in 2025, and other spotlight projects are described as being developed or recently launched. Participants favor practical short-term efficiency improvements and rapid experiments because the technology is changing quickly and its best uses remain uncertain. Recommendation 7 distinguishes near-term development of measurable self-help improvements from longer-term replication and uptake; that timeline applies to emerging-technology self-help broadly, not solely AI.

pts.k: Expected benefits are qualified by reliability, confidentiality, safe experimentation, organizational buy-in and adequate implementation support.
pts.d: Participants identify inaccurate AI information, security concerns and ethical or confidentiality risks, including those arising from meeting transcription. Nate Vogel reports practitioners' concern that tools are not yet good enough for generating factual information. LSC proposes secure sandboxes, privacy and governance policies, training, shared implementation guidance and impact assessment to enable responsible adoption. Cat Moon suggests sandboxes would allow non-IT experts to explore AI without jeopardizing data security. The report advocates these safeguards but does not supply a detailed human-verification protocol or measured reliability threshold.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The intended beneficiaries are low-income people with unmet civil legal needs, legal aid staff and self-represented litigants, particularly people facing geographic or accessibility barriers.
pts.d: The provider segment is LSC's network of 130 independent nonprofit civil legal services organizations and the wider access-to-justice community, rather than commercial law firms or enterprise legal buyers. Attorneys, intake workers and administrative staff are expected to gain workflow support and capacity. Clients are expected to receive faster routing and more accessible information, while unrepresented people may gain guidance and document assistance. The Louisiana project particularly targets rural callers; North Carolina's Justice Hub targets a state population of around three million eligible residents, not three million demonstrated users. Broader self-help recommendations emphasize multilingual resources, literacy and disability accessibility, and tools for community justice workers providing legal information and limited-scope services. Courts, funders, law schools and technology vendors are identified as collaborators needed to implement and scale the changes.
